summary: Specifies a packet format that can carry multiple messages, for use by routing protocols in mobile ad hoc networks. This is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 7631 and RFC 8245.

eli5.summary: In a network of moving devices, many small notes can be bundled into one envelope. This memo defines how the envelope and its notes are laid out.

questions: what is an address block in manet
subtitle: A compact, extensible packet and message layout that MANET routing protocols can share.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc network routing protocols run over limited wireless links, so they need a compact, extensible way to pack several protocol messages and lists of addresses into one transmission.
tldr.mechanism: A packet holds a small header and zero or more messages. Each message has a header, a block of TLV attributes and Address Blocks that compress shared address parts, each followed by its own TLVs.
tldr.outcome: It specifies syntax only, not a protocol. It is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 7631 and RFC 8245.

today: RFC 5444 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7631 and RFC 8245, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: A Shared Format for MANET Routing
sections.content:
RFC 5444 specifies the syntax of a packet format for carrying multiple routing protocol messages between MANET (Mobile Ad hoc NETwork) routers. It does not describe a protocol; any mobile ad hoc network routing protocol may use it. It was inspired by and extended from the format used by OLSR (RFC 3626).

The four design goals are generic parsing logic, extensibility (new messages and TLVs can be identified and skipped), efficiency (shared address bits are stored once and several messages share a packet), and separation of forwarding from processing (duplicate detection and scoped forwarding can use the Message Header alone).

Because MANETs often run on wireless interfaces of limited to moderate capacity, the format trades off efficiency, extensibility and ease of use. All numbers use network byte order.
sections.eli5: Wireless gadgets that move around have little room to talk, so they need a short, tidy way of writing messages that everyone understands.

sections.title: Packets and Messages
sections.content:
A packet is a Packet Header followed by zero or more messages. The header has a 4-bit version (this document specifies version 0), a 4-bit flags field, an optional 16-bit packet sequence number and an optional TLV block. The packet length is not carried; the network layer is assumed to deliver the exact payload length. Parsing ends when all octets of the datagram are used.

A message is a Message Header, a Message TLV Block and zero or more pairs of an Address Block with its TLV Block. The header always has an 8-bit msg-type, 4 flag bits, a 4-bit msg-addr-length and a 16-bit msg-size. Four optional fields follow: originator address, hop limit, hop count and sequence number, each present only if its flag bit is set.

msg-addr-length is the address length in octets minus 1, so it is 3 for IPv4 and 15 for IPv6. All addresses in one message have the same size.
sections.eli5: A packet is an envelope with a small label on the front. Inside there can be no notes, one note or many, and each note has its own short heading.

sections.title: Address Blocks
sections.content:
An Address Block lists addresses compactly. Each address is split into Head:Mid:Tail. All addresses in a block share the same Head and the same Tail, and each has its own Mid. Head and Tail may be empty, and a tail of all zero octets can be signaled with a flag instead of being sent.

The block starts with an 8-bit num-addr (which MUST NOT be zero) and an 8-bit flags field. Optional parts follow: head length and head, tail length and tail, the Mid of each address, and then prefix lengths. A block can have no prefix lengths, one prefix length for all addresses, or one per address, so it can mix addresses and address prefixes. A prefix length greater than 8 times the address length makes the block malformed.

For example, in IPv4 the addresses a.b.c.d, a.b.e.f and a.b.g.h share a two-octet head, and the RFC encodes the block as 11 octets: 3 128 2 a b c d e f g h.
sections.eli5: If everyone on your street shares the same first part of their address, you write that part once and then only list each house number.

sections.title: TLVs and TLV Blocks
sections.content:
A TLV (type-length-value) attaches an attribute to a packet, a message, or addresses in an Address Block. A parser can skip a TLV it does not understand. TLVs sit in TLV Blocks, each starting with a 16-bit length of the TLVs that follow. There are three kinds: Packet TLVs, Message TLVs and Address Block TLVs.

Each TLV has an 8-bit type and an 8-bit flags field. Optional parts are a type extension (the full type is 256 times the type plus the extension), one or two index fields, and a length and value. The length is 8 bits, or 16 bits if the extended length flag is set. An Address Block TLV can apply to one address, a continuous range of addresses or all addresses of the block, and its value can be one value for all of them or one value per address.

A protocol using this format MUST define how to handle inconsistent TLVs, such as two TLVs of the same type with different values on the same entity, and the order in which TLVs are processed.
sections.eli5: A TLV is a sticky note that says what kind of note it is, how long it is, and what it says. If you do not know the kind, you can skip it using the length.

sections.title: Malformed Elements
sections.content: An element is malformed if it cannot be parsed according to its syntax, including when too few octets are available. A malformed element in the Packet Header means the whole packet MUST be silently discarded, and its messages MUST NOT be processed or forwarded. A malformed element inside a message (its TLV block, an Address Block or an Address Block TLV block) means that message MUST be silently discarded and neither processed nor forwarded.
sections.eli5: If a letter is scribbled so badly you cannot read it, you throw it away quietly instead of guessing what it meant.

sections.title: Intended Usage: Flooding and Multiplexing
sections.content:
Messages are meant to be forwarded over one or more logical hops, in a new packet for each hop. For scope-limited flooding, the originator address, sequence number (wraps from 65535 to 0), message type, hop limit and hop count are used. The originator address, sequence number and message type together identify a message for duplicate suppression. A router should decrease the hop limit by 1 when forwarding and discard at 0. It should increase the hop count by 1 and discard at 255.

Appendix A describes multiplexing. Messages from different protocols may share one packet, so a multiplexing and demultiplexing process MUST exist. Each message type has an owning protocol, and incoming messages are delivered only to the owner or silently discarded. Packet sequence numbers also wrap from 65535 to 0.
sections.eli5: Each note carries a counter of how many hands it can still pass through, so it cannot wander forever. Notes from different games sharing an envelope are handed only to the game they belong to.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes a format rather than a protocol, so it specifies no security requirements, but it enables some mechanisms. A cryptographic signature in a Message TLV can give end-to-end authentication of a forwarded message, computed with the hop count and hop limit set to 0. A signature in a Packet TLV can give hop-by-hop authentication. Confidentiality would normally come from the link layer or IP layer, or from encrypting a TLV value, which the protocol MUST then define.

IANA registries cover Message Types, Packet TLV Types, Message TLV Types and Address Block TLV Types, with type extension registries beneath them. In the TLV registries, types 0 to 127 are common to all message types, 128 to 223 are message-type-specific, and 224 to 255 are for experimental use. Registration is by Expert Review.
sections.eli5: The envelope itself has no lock. If a game wants one, it can add its own signature or secret code on the note.

items.title: Packet
items.text: Packet Header with optional sequence number and TLV block, then zero or more messages.

items.title: Message
items.text: Message Header, a TLV block, then Address Blocks each followed by a TLV block.

items.title: Address Block
items.text: Addresses compressed into shared Head and Tail with individual Mids.

items.title: TLV
items.text: Type, flags and optional extension, index, length and value.

data.title: Three addresses sharing a two-octet head
data.code:
To include a.b.c.d, a.b.e.f and a.b.g.h:
  head-length = 2, tail-length = 0, mid-length = 2
  addr-flags has ahashead set (value 128)
Address Block: 3 128 2 a b c d e f g h  (11 octets)
